547.title: White, red and black mountains
547.hook: mountains with streaks of white, red and black, and those with knowledge stand in awe (35:27–28)
547.howItsDone: Muslim scholars often cite 35:28 to describe the link between learning and reverence, and many Muslims count reflecting on creation (tafakkur) as a form of worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mathna, the angels' wings in twos, threes and fours. Your line was he adds to creation as he wills.
screen: `HE ADDS TO CREATION AS HE WILLS.`

segments.voice: Drive through a road cut, where the highway slices straight through a hill, and you'll see it: the rock in bands. A pale stripe, a rusty red one, a dark one, stacked like a layer cake. Most people glance and keep driving. A geologist pulls over. To her, each band is a chapter: mud, ash, iron and a long stretch of time. Surah Fatir points at exactly those stripes, and then says who, looking at them, feels the most awe. It isn't the person you might expect.

Verse twenty-seven asks: haven't you seen that Allah sends water from the sky, and with it brings out fruits of different colors? And in the mountains, streaks, white and red, of different hues, and others jet black. The word for the streaks, judad, means tracks or paths, lines running through the rock. The word for the deepest black, gharabib, is linked in the dictionaries to ghurab, the raven. Verse twenty-eight keeps going: and people, and animals, and cattle, also of different colors. A whole palette, from fruit to stone to faces. Then the line the passage was building to. Pickthall: "The erudite among His bondmen fear Allah alone." The Arabic word is al-'ulama', those who know. Today it usually means religious scholars, and many read the verse that way. But notice where it sits: right after rocks, rain, fruit, animals and human skin. Some commentators point out that the knowledge here can include knowing creation, looking long enough at the stripes in a mountain to be moved by them. The verb is yakhsha, from khashya, a fear that's really awe: the trembling respect of someone who understands how great a thing is. Some people assume that the more you know, the less wonder is left. The verse says the opposite: the ones who know are the ones who stand in awe.

Find a stone, from a garden, a sidewalk, a windowsill, or a countertop if that's what you have, and hold it close, looking for colors you missed at first: a vein, a speck, a band. Turn it over, and think about how long it took to become what it is. If no stone is near, look at the back of your own hand the same way.
White. The first color named in the mountains' streaks in Surah Fatir: white, red and raven-black, a palette the verse says moves those who know to awe. Today's word.
Your line: knowledge brings awe. White, red, and raven-black. Tomorrow, the heart of the book.

548.title: Ya-Sin, heart of the book
548.hook: often recited for the dying and on Thursday nights in many communities
548.tomorrow: The man from the city's edge
548.howItsDone: In many Muslim communities Ya-Sin is recited beside the dying, at graves, and on Thursday evenings before Friday; scholars differ on the strength of the hadith behind these customs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: white, red and black mountains, and those who know standing in awe. Your line was knowledge brings awe.

A hospital room, late. A grandmother is very ill, and the family has gathered. Someone opens a small, worn booklet, or a phone, and begins to recite in Arabic, softly, steadily. In a mosque across town, it's Thursday evening, and a circle of people is reciting the same words. In a cemetery, someone stands by a grave and reads it again. In many Muslim communities, this is the surah people reach for at the edges of life. It begins with two letters: Ya. Sin.

Surah thirty-six, eighty-three verses. Its name is its first verse: two Arabic letters, ya and sin, said by themselves, like the disconnected letters that open a number of surahs. What they mean, many scholars say, Allah knows best. Some say Ya-Sin is a name for the Prophet ﷺ, and it's also a boy's name. The text doesn't say. Then, Pickthall: "By the wise Qur'an, Lo! thou art of those sent". An oath on the book itself, and a reassurance to the Prophet that he's a real messenger. Why is it called the heart of the Qur'an? A hadith in the collection of al-Tirmidhi says everything has a heart, and the heart of the Qur'an is Ya-Sin. Another, in Abu Dawud, says recite Ya-Sin over your dying. The honest part: many hadith scholars grade both reports as weak in their chains. Others accept them, or point to the surah's content. And the content speaks to what a family at a bedside may want to hear: it says the messengers were true, that the dead will be raised, that the One who made a person the first time can make them again. Its closing verses ask, can't He who created the heavens and the earth create their like? At a bedside, that's not abstract theology. It's a promise said aloud in a hard room. So Ya-Sin earned its place in many communities on two grounds: reports some accept and some question, and a message everyone can hear. Over the next three days, this path opens it.

549.title: The man from the city's edge
549.hook: a man runs from the edge of the city to tell his people to follow the messengers (36:20–27)
549.howItsDone: Muslim preachers often tell the story of the man from the city's edge as an example of courage and of sincere goodwill toward people who reject you; tradition names him Habib al-Najjar.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ya-Sin, the surah families reach for at a bedside. Your line was the heart of the book.

A town meeting has turned ugly. Messengers have come, first two, then a third to back them up, and the townspeople aren't having it. You're just bad luck, they say. Stop, or we'll stone you. Voices are rising in the square. And then, from the far side of town, from the outskirts, someone is running. Not walking, running. He's not a messenger. He's not a leader. The Qur'an doesn't even give his name. He just couldn't stay home.

Surah Ya-Sin, verse twenty. Pickthall: "And there came from the uttermost part of the city a man running. He cried: O my people! Follow those who have been sent!" The uttermost part of the city: the edge, far from power. Running: he didn't wait to see how it would turn out. His first argument is simple. Verse twenty-one: follow those who ask no payment from you, and who are rightly guided. They want nothing from you; that's how you can tell. Then he speaks about himself: why shouldn't I worship the One who created me, to whom you'll all return? I believe in your Lord, so listen to me. The Qur'an doesn't narrate what happened next. It cuts straight to verse twenty-six: it was said to him, enter the Garden. Many commentators understand from this that his people killed him. And his first words in paradise are the most surprising part: if only my people knew how my Lord has forgiven me and honored me. No anger. No wish for revenge. He still wants them to make it. A saying in the commentaries, attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, puts it this way: he gave his people good advice while he was alive, and he wished them well after they killed him. Tradition calls him Habib the carpenter, and many place the town at Antioch, but the Qur'an names neither. He's the man from the edge, and that's enough.

Think of someone in your life, at work, in your family, online, who's saying something true and getting no support. Picture yourself, like the man from the edge, walking over to stand next to them, and hear what you'd say, kept short, the way he did. Rest there a moment.

Your line: he came running. No name in the text, only the running. See you tomorrow.

550.title: The sun on its course
550.hook: the sun runs to its resting place, the moon returns like an old palm stalk (36:38–40)
550.howItsDone: The Islamic calendar is lunar: each month traditionally begins with the sighting of the new crescent, and many communities still send people to look for it, especially for Ramadan and the two Eids.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Habib, the man who ran from the city's edge. Your line was he came running.

Go outside on the first evening after a new moon, right after sunset, and look low in the west. If the sky is clear, you might catch it: a crescent so thin it's barely there, curved like a fingernail clipping, pale yellow. Muslims have long climbed rooftops and hills to look for exactly that sliver, because it starts the month, Ramadan included. Surah Ya-Sin has its own picture for a thin, curved moon, something anyone living among date palms would know.

Verses thirty-seven to forty are a set of signs. The night, stripped off the day like a skin, leaving people in darkness. Then the sun, which runs toward a resting place appointed for it, by the measuring of the Mighty, the Wise. Then the moon: Allah has set stations for it, until it returns like al-'urjun al-qadim, the old date stalk. Picture a date palm. The stalk that holds the cluster, once it's old and dried, curves over, thin and yellowish. That's the waning crescent. People who lived among palms would have seen the shape instantly. Then verse forty. Pickthall: "It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day. They float each in an orbit." The verb for float is yasbahun, the word for swimming. Each one swims along its own path. Nothing crashes. Nothing cuts in line. Where the sun's resting place is, the verse doesn't explain. A hadith in Bukhari has Abu Dharr asking the Prophet ﷺ about it, and scholars have read that answer in different ways, some as the sun's submission to Allah, some as the end of time. The Qur'an's own point is plainer: all of this keeps its measure, the sun its run, the moon its stations, night and day their turns. It's called a sign, something to look at and think about. And for many Muslims the calendar still turns on it: a month begins when someone looks up and sees the thin crescent again.

551.title: "Be," and it is
551.hook: His command, when He wills a thing, is only to say be, and it is (36:82)
551.howItsDone: Muslims often say 'kun fa-yakun' when speaking of Allah's power to bring about what seems impossible, and the closing verses of Ya-Sin are commonly recited at funerals and by the dying.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ya-Sin's moon, returning like an old date stalk. Your line was each swims in its orbit.

A man walks up holding an old bone, dry and crumbling, picked up from some forgotten grave. He crushes it in his fist, and the dust falls between his fingers. Then he asks the question that's been his whole argument: who could bring this back to life? Anyone who's stood at a funeral has asked a version of it. Surah Ya-Sin ends by answering him, and the answer comes down to a single word of two letters in Arabic.

Verse seventy-eight. He coins a comparison for Us, Allah says, and forgets his own creation. He asks, who will revive bones once they've rotted away? Verse seventy-nine answers: the One who brought them into being the first time will revive them. He knows every creation. The man forgot that he himself was once nothing. If starting a person from nothing was possible, starting again from dust is no harder. Verse eighty adds a picture: the One who makes fire for you from the green tree. Something living and wet, and out of it comes flame. Then the line the whole surah has been walking toward. Pickthall: "But His command, when He intendeth a thing, is only that He saith unto it: Be! and it is." In Arabic: kun, fa-yakun. Kun is two letters, kaf and nun. Muslims understand this as the Qur'an's way of describing Allah's power, not a picture of Allah speaking like a person: no effort, no delay, no materials needed. The Qur'an uses the phrase in several places: for the creation of the heavens and earth, for the birth of 'Isa, Jesus, and here, for raising the dead. Then the last verse of Ya-Sin: glory to Him in whose hand is the dominion of all things, and to Him you'll be brought back. This is why the surah is read beside the dying. The question in that room is the man's question: can this come back? Ya-Sin's answer is the first answer again: the One who began it from nothing can begin it again.

In the verse, there's no gap between the command and the thing; a life is full of gaps. Think of one task you've been putting off, a call, a form, an apology, and picture only its very first step, small enough for a minute. If you pray, you can say bismillah over it, and sit quietly with the decision made.
Be. Kun, the word of Allah's command in Ya-Sin's closing verses: He says to a thing be, and it is, and so He can raise the dead. Today's word.

552.title: The ranks
552.hook: by those ranged in ranks, the angels, and the believers in rows for prayer (37:1)
552.howItsDone: Before congregational prayer, the imam often tells the people to straighten their rows; worshippers stand shoulder to shoulder and foot to foot, filling the front rows first.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kun, be, and it is, the close of Ya-Sin. Your line was no harder the second time.

Watch the start of a Friday prayer in a big mosque, from the balcony if you can. Hundreds of people are milling around, finding spots, greeting friends. Then the call to stand comes. People step forward, shoulder to shoulder, heel to heel. Gaps close. Lines straighten. In a few seconds, a crowd becomes rows, as straight as if someone had drawn them with a ruler. Surah thirty-seven opens with an oath on exactly that kind of line, though the first ones it means aren't on earth.

The surah is called As-Saffat. Its first verse is an oath: wa's-saffati saffa, by those ranged in ranks. The root, s-f-f, means a row, a line. Many commentators say these are angels, standing in rows before their Lord, waiting for His command. Near the end of the same surah, in verses commentators read as the angels speaking, they describe themselves that way: we are those who stand in ranks, and we are those who glorify. So the first rows aren't human at all. Then the hadith brings the picture down to earth. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ asks his companions: won't you line up the way the angels line up before their Lord? They ask how the angels line up. He says: they complete the front rows first, and they stand close together. Another hadith, in both Bukhari and Muslim, says: straighten your rows, for straightening the rows is part of establishing and completing the prayer. So the row isn't only tidiness; many Muslims understand it as copying the angels. And it does something. In a row, the rich man and the driver stand shoulder to shoulder. Nobody has a reserved seat. Whoever arrives first fills the front. The line itself teaches something about equality before Allah, without anyone having to say it.

Sit or stand tall, feet even, shoulders level, as if you were in a row with someone on either side. If something near you is crooked, books on a shelf, shoes by the door, straighten one line of them, slowly, with care. Then return to stillness and picture the rows: angels before their Lord, and people shoulder to shoulder below.
The ranks. As-Saffat, the rows: angels standing before their Lord, and believers who straighten their lines for prayer to stand the way the angels stand. Today's word.
Your line: in ranks. The first rows were in heaven, and the mosque floor copies them. Until tomorrow.

553.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite the prayer of Yunus (la ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu mina z-zalimin) in times of distress, and make tasbih (subhanallah) part of daily remembrance after each prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ranks, angels in rows, and people copying them in prayer. Your line was in ranks.

What if Yunus had never come out of the fish? Surah As-Saffat has a sentence about exactly that. It tells his story again, briefly: the prophet who left in anger, the ship, the lots, the great fish. This path met him back in year one, with the three darknesses and the prayer he cried out from inside. But As-Saffat slips in a sentence found only here. An if. If one thing about Yunus had been different, the story wouldn't have ended on a beach under a gourd vine. It wouldn't have ended at all.

As-Saffat gives the story in ten verses. Yunus was one of the messengers. He fled to the laden ship. Lots were drawn, and he lost. The fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy. Then verses one forty-three and forty-four. Pickthall: "And had he not been one of those who glorify (Allah) He would have tarried in its belly till the day when they are raised". That's the if. The Arabic is mina'l-musabbihin, one of those who glorify, from the same root as subhanallah. Commentators read this two ways, and both are worth keeping. Some say it means his glorifying inside the fish, the cry from year one: there's no god but You, glory to You, I was one of the wrongdoers. Others, reported from early commentators, say it means the glorifying he'd done for years before the fish: prayer and remembrance in easy times, remembered for him in the hard one. A hadith sounds the same note. The Prophet ﷺ told the young Ibn 'Abbas: know Allah in times of ease, and He will know you in times of hardship. On that second reading, the if isn't only about the right words at the worst moment. It's about years of glorifying that came before the dark. The week ran on the same thread: the man from the city's edge ran without waiting, the sun and moon keep a measure set long before, and the rows close up because people have practiced lining up.
screen: `IN THE FISH, OR LONG BEFORE IT?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a small tight spot from this week, a deadline, an argument, a worry, and feel where it sits in your body. If you're Muslim, or want to try, say subhanallah, glory be to Allah, quietly, a few times while you hold it; if not, simply name the tight spot and breathe slowly beside it. Starting while things are calm is the point, so the habit is there later.
Yunus. The prophet in the fish, who, As-Saffat says, would have stayed there until the Day of Rising if he hadn't been one who glorifies Allah. Today's word.
Your line: glorifying got him out. In ease first, then in the dark. Another week, done.

fork.setup: you're Yunus, in the dark inside the fish. As-Saffat says one thing about you made the difference. what was it?
options: you were a prophet's son.
you were one of those who glorify Allah.
you had been right about your people.
fork.reveal: he was one of those who glorify. commentators debate whether it means inside the fish or the years before; many keep both.

original.note: Arabic: of those who glorify, the root of subhanallah.

trapdoor: what you thought: Yunus was saved by one prayer in the dark.
what it means: As-Saffat says he was saved because he was one who glorifies, and that may include years before the fish.

what a scholar hears: 37:143–144's conditional is read by some as his tasbih in the fish (21:87) and by others as his earlier worship; the Ibn 'Abbas hadith 'know Allah in ease' is often cited alongside.
recall: the ant who warned the others

chat.says: What does As-Saffat say saved Yunus from staying inside the fish?
options: That he was one of those who glorify God, in the fish or in years before.
That the sailors prayed for him once they had thrown him overboard.
That he promised to go back and finish preaching, so he was released.
chat.meaning: As-Saffat 37:143–144: had he not been one of those who glorify, he'd have stayed in its belly. Commentators read that as in the fish, or before.

Yunus.meaning: the prophet swallowed by the great fish

Ibn 'Abbas.meaning: a young Companion the Prophet advised
